lessons.title: Technology Always Arrives in Waves
lessons.key_idea: Once a general-purpose technology works, it spreads, gets cheaper and becomes nearly impossible to stop, as history repeatedly shows.

lessons.title: AI and Synthetic Biology Lead the Wave
lessons.key_idea: Artificial intelligence and the ability to engineer life are the twin technologies driving the next wave, and they amplify each other.

lessons.title: Four Traits That Make This Wave Different
lessons.key_idea: This wave is uniquely hard to control because it is asymmetric, hyper-evolving, omni-use and increasingly autonomous.

lessons.title: Why Nobody Wants to Slow Down
lessons.key_idea: Powerful incentives like profit, national rivalry and curiosity push the wave forward, while pessimism aversion stops us from facing the risks.

lessons.title: The Nation-State Under Pressure
lessons.key_idea: The wave strains the bargain in which states provide order and security, empowering both tiny bad actors and giant centralised powers.

lessons.title: The Dilemma: Catastrophe or Dystopia
lessons.key_idea: Letting the wave run free risks catastrophe, but controlling it too tightly risks authoritarian surveillance, and both outcomes are dangerous.

lessons.title: Walking the Narrow Path to Containment
lessons.key_idea: No single fix will work, but many layered measures, from safety research and audits to laws, alliances and culture, can together keep the wave in check.

plan.title: The Coming Wave
plan.author: Mustafa Suleyman with Michael Bhaskar
plan.confidence_note: I know the book's core arguments and structure well, including the containment problem, the wave's four features, the dilemma, and the ten steps, though I won't rely on finer anecdotal details.
plan.one_liner: A DeepMind co-founder warns that AI and biotech are coming fast, and asks whether we can control them.
plan.summary: Mustafa Suleyman, a co-founder of DeepMind, argues that humanity is about to be hit by a new wave of technology, led by artificial intelligence and synthetic biology. History shows that general-purpose technologies spread relentlessly once they work, getting cheaper and more accessible until almost anyone can use them. This wave is different because its tools are cheap, fast-evolving, useful for nearly everything, and increasingly autonomous. That creates what he calls the containment problem: how do we keep control of technologies that could empower tiny groups to cause enormous harm? He warns of a grim dilemma. Failing to contain the wave risks catastrophe, while clamping down too hard risks a surveillance-heavy dystopia. His answer is a narrow path of layered steps, from safety engineering and audits to laws, alliances and culture, that together could make containment possible.
